rule_changes_ranked.name: Fix _nearest_free_goal push direction/target (goal-projection convention)
rule_changes_ranked.location: src/core/runner/gt_battery.py::_nearest_free_goal (also mirrored in core/heads/instruction.py's real-nav goto/via projection)
rule_changes_ranked.mechanism: Anchor AABB is already within the 0.8 m arrival tolerance of the GT path, but the rubric's projected stop point (nearest-free-goal push off the anchor's own or a neighbouring obstacle's footprint edge, clearance 0.4 m, bounded 2.5 m push) lands the goal OUTSIDE tolerance. The push is blind to the GT path/approach direction -- it always moves to the nearest AABB edge, which is frequently the wrong side relative to where the demonstrator actually stood. Fix: bias the push toward the side of the anchor nearest the incoming leg's prior goal (or, cheaper, clamp push distance harder / prefer the raw centroid over a push that increases distance to any reachable point) so the projected stop point never moves further from the anchor's own reachable neighbourhood than the raw centroid did.

rule_changes_ranked.name: Widen/soften the arrival-tolerance convention for near-miss stop points
rule_changes_ranked.mechanism: Anchor AABB itself sits 0.8-1.5 m from the GT path (not touching it), and the projected goal is not appreciably closer -- these are not push-direction bugs, they are a systematic 'the demonstrator stopped near but not AT the object, at a distance the current stop-point convention (project onto/off the AABB edge) does not reach.' Needs a convention change: project the goal toward the GT-path side of the room / a fixed standoff distance from the anchor along the approach direction, not just off the nearest colliding obstacle.

rule_changes_ranked.name: Fix superlative-anchor (closest_to/farthest_from) resolution
rule_changes_ranked.mechanism: The clause's own reference anchor (e.g. 'the hookah', 'the easel', 'the chair') resolves ambiguously when the scene has multiple candidates for it, or the closest_to/farthest_from Euclidean ranking of survivors disagrees with which candidate the demonstrator actually treated as satisfying the superlative -- picking the wrong same-class instance outright. Needs per-case tracing of the reference-anchor resolution (is 'hookah' itself picking the wrong instance) before a single global fix can be specified; likely several distinct root causes bucketed under one symptom.

rule_changes_ranked.name: Fix ON/WITH relation-clause fallback ranking
rule_changes_ranked.mechanism: A residual instance of the same on()/with() hard-gate-vs-soft-score gap documented for issue #59 (7-leg bucket, since partly fixed): the relation clause still fails as a HARD filter for the correct candidate (footprint/height edge cases) and the category-only fallback's soft ranking (_relaxed_relation_order) still does not consistently prefer the geometrically-correct candidate. Needs auditing the specific on()/with() failures per leg (chinese_room tea table, home_building_1 coffee table, home_building_2 magazine-on-ottoman, japanese_room table-with-vase, studio vase-on-cabinet) to find the next edge case the #59 fix didn't cover.

rule_changes_ranked.name: Redefine corridor_between leg arrival point (not the raw gate midpoint)
rule_changes_ranked.mechanism: Both of a corridor leg's anchors can sit right on the GT path (AABB dist 0.0 m and ~1.4-1.8 m) while the straight-line MIDPOINT between them is 1.7-1.9 m off the path -- the demonstrator threaded the gap at an angle, not through the segment midpoint. Fix: score corridor_between legs by whether the GT path crosses the gate SEGMENT (or a widened gate band) anywhere, not by distance to its midpoint; or move the rubric goal to the path's actual closest crossing point on the segment.

rule_changes_ranked.name: Fix bare-noun category tie-break (no relation clause at all)
rule_changes_ranked.mechanism: livingroom_3's 'the cabinet' (no disambiguating clause in this leg) resolves via plain tier-priority/instance-id tie-break among multiple same-class cabinets; the correct one (a TV cabinet, per the scene's role in the sentence) is not the top-ranked survivor. A single-leg symptom; not enough evidence here to prescribe a general rule beyond 'when multiple bare-noun survivors exist, prefer the one closest to elsewhere already established in the route' as a candidate heuristic.
